We shut down our EU expansion after seven months. Cost us about $400k.

The thing nobody tells you: the hard part wasn't GDPR or the entity setup. It was that our sales motion assumed a 3-week eval cycle and German mid-market runs 11 weeks with a works council review in the middle. Our AEs were comped on a quota that made that math impossible, so they churned.

We could have found that out with four customer calls before hiring anyone. We did the calls after.

Reopening next year with a longer cycle baked into comp.

Our p99 latency was 340ms and our p50 was 12ms. That gap is the whole story.

The obvious guess was garbage collection, and it wasn't. We spent two days on GC logs before someone noticed the slow requests correlated with a specific shard, not a specific time.

Turned out one customer had 2.3M rows in a table we'd assumed would hold a few thousand, and a query with no index on the filter column. It had been fine for a year because that customer had 400 rows when they signed up.

Adding the index took p99 to 19ms. The two days were spent looking at the wrong distribution — we were averaging across shards, so the one bad shard vanished into the mean.

If your p50 and p99 disagree that badly, stop looking at time series and start looking at which key is slow.

Depends what you mean by "doesn't scale."

If you're hitting connection limits, pgbouncer in transaction mode fixes it and takes an afternoon. If you're hitting write throughput, that's a different problem and pgbouncer won't help at all.

I ran Postgres at about 40k writes/sec on a single primary for two years. It was fine. The thing that eventually forced a change wasn't throughput, it was that our largest table hit a point where any schema migration took a maintenance window we couldn't afford.

So: what's actually breaking?

Three things this week.

The Postgres 18 release notes have a line about `NOT NULL NOT VALID` that I think most people will miss. It lets you add a not-null constraint without the full table scan, then validate later. If you've been avoiding that migration on a big table, it's now cheap.

I was wrong about something I wrote in March. I said the new pricing on Fly.io made it uncompetitive for small apps. I'd misread the free allowance — it's per-org, not per-app, which changes the math for anyone running more than two services. Sorry.
